input: Liquid-liquid extraction is a widely used and highly effective technique for separating components, and in this case it has been applied to the recovery of phenol from an aqueous stream by contacting the stream with an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient, which is defined as the ratio of the phenol concentration in the organic phase to that in the aqueous phase, has a value of 1.33 at 25 °C, and the design that has been developed makes use of 3 countercurrent stages in order to achieve the desired separation. According to the predictions that have been made, something like 92% of the phenol present in the feed can be recovered in this way, which represents a very respectable level of performance, and a recovery of 92% is the figure around which the economics of the separation will ultimately be judged. The phenol which is recovered leaves in the extract, from which it must subsequently be separated from the solvent, while the solvent itself has to be recovered and recycled if the process is to be operated economically, and the treated aqueous stream still retains whatever phenol has not been extracted. It is also to be borne in mind that none of this downstream duty is reflected in the stage calculation itself, which is concerned solely with the contacting section. It should nevertheless be kept in mind that these predictions are based on certain assumptions that have been made for the sake of convenience, in particular the assumption that every stage behaves as a perfect equilibrium stage and the assumption that the mutual solubility of the two solvents can be neglected, and neither of these assumptions has yet been properly checked against the behaviour of the actual solvents that will be used in the process, so a degree of caution is appropriate when the figures are used.
target: Liquid-liquid extraction recovers phenol from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent at a predicted recovery of 92% of the phenol in the feed. The design basis is a distribution coefficient (organic over aqueous) of 1.33 at 25 °C and 3 countercurrent stages. The coefficient fixes how the phenol divides between the phases at each stage, and the stage count converts that division into the overall recovery: each stage leaves a smaller fraction of the phenol in the aqueous stream than the stage before, and the raffinate leaving the last stage holds the unrecovered remainder. Countercurrent contact is what makes the stage count effective, because the leanest solvent meets the leanest aqueous stream and the driving force for transfer is held along the cascade rather than spent at the feed end. The prediction assumes equilibrium stages and negligible mutual solubility, and neither assumption has been checked on the actual solvents. A stage that falls short of equilibrium delivers less transfer than the design credits it with, and mutual solubility moves solvent into the raffinate and phenol-bearing water into the extract, changing both the recovery and the load on the separation steps that follow. The recovered phenol leaves in the extract and is separated from the solvent in the steps that follow the cascade; the solvent is itself recovered for reuse, and the treated aqueous stream retains the phenol the stages did not take up, so the extraction sets the duty of both the product recovery and the effluent treatment that stand downstream of it in the operating plant. None of that downstream duty appears in the stage calculation. The 92% figure is therefore the recovery of the design model, stated on its stated basis; the recovery of the installed unit is bounded by it only until the two assumptions have been tested.
